Source: https://docs.aivax.net/docs/web-foundation/fetch-and-ocr.html

# Fetch and OCR

Fetch and OCR extracts readable text from web pages and supported documents so applications and agents can use their content for summaries, analysis, or knowledge workflows. The Fetch API can also convert the extracted text into structured JSON using a schema you provide. Use [Web Search](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/web-foundation/web-search.md) first if you need to discover sources rather than read a known URL.

Web pages are processed to remove markup and non-content elements. Document extraction and optical character recognition (OCR) make supported non-text content available as text. Review extracted content before relying on it: scan quality, complex layouts, and tables can affect the result. For an end-to-end walkthrough with a code example, see [how to extract text from a URL, scanned PDF or image for an LLM pipeline](https://aivax.net/blog/fetch-messy-web-to-text/).

## What you can extract

| Content | Supported formats | Extracted content |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Web pages | HTML, XHTML | Readable page content, such as articles, documentation, and product information, with markup and non-content elements removed. JavaScript and CSS are rendered before extraction. |
| Plain text and Markdown | TXT, Markdown | The document's text, including existing Markdown formatting. |
| PDFs | PDF | Text from digital documents and OCR text from scanned pages. Mixed PDFs can combine direct text extraction with OCR where needed. |
| Images containing text | PNG, JPEG, WebP, TIFF, BMP | Recognized text from screenshots, scanned documents, receipts, and other images with legible writing. |
| Word-processing documents | DOC, DOCX, ODT, RTF | Document text converted into a readable textual representation. |
| Presentations | PPT, PPTX, ODP | Textual slide content. |
| Spreadsheets and tabular files | XLSX, ODS, CSV | Cell and row content as text, for downstream reading or analysis. |
| E-books | EPUB | The publication's text. |

For example, you can fetch an online article, read a PDF manual, extract text from a receipt image, or turn a spreadsheet into text for an agent to analyze. Provide a URL that returns the actual page or file, not a sharing page that requires a login. When submitting a data URI through the API, declare the content's correct MIME type.

The result is extracted text, not a pixel-perfect copy of the original document. Do not assume that layout, table structure, charts, or embedded images will be reproduced exactly. Spreadsheet extraction does not execute formulas or macros.

For a worked example that fetches a PDF, extracts its text, and turns it into RAG-ready chunks, see [PDF to Markdown for RAG](https://aivax.net/blog/pdf-to-markdown-for-rag-chunks-jsonl/).

## Fetch API vs. Media Descriptions

Use the **Fetch API to extract existing text**. Use [Media Descriptions](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/data-processing/media-descriptions.md) to **interpret media with AI**, optionally guided by what your application needs to learn from it.

| | Fetch API | Media Descriptions |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Main purpose | Retrieve readable text from pages and documents, using OCR for supported images and scanned PDFs. | Generate descriptions or extract information from images, PDFs, audio, and video using AI. |
| Output | Extracted text, optional schema-guided JSON generated from that text, processing-unit usage, and per-item errors. | Model-generated content focused by your guidance, which can describe visual or audiovisual information beyond the text present in the source. |
| Images and PDFs | Read text, such as the words on a receipt or the paragraphs in a manual. | Describe visual content or interpret a document, such as explaining a diagram or identifying information relevant to a question. |
| Audio and video | Not an audio/video understanding or transcription API. | Analyze audio and video content. For a dedicated speech-to-text workflow, use [Audio Transcriptions](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/generations/audio-transcriptions.md). |
| Billing | Extraction processing units (PUs), with plan-dependent allowances and rates. Optional JSON conversion is billed separately and is not covered by the extraction allowance. | AI usage charges under Media Descriptions pricing; Fetch PU allowances do not replace these charges. |

For a PDF report, choose Fetch when you need its text for indexing or later analysis. Choose Media Descriptions when you need an explanation of its charts or a guided interpretation of the content. For a receipt image, Fetch reads the printed text; Media Descriptions can interpret the receipt according to your extraction guidance.

When you need specific fields as JSON from text, images, or PDFs, rather than the document's full text, use [Extraction](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/data-processing/extraction.md). It reads the fields directly from each document and bills only input tokens, while Fetch converts to JSON from the extracted text as a separate, inference-priced step. Fetch remains the choice for web pages, other document formats, larger files, and workflows that also need the full text.

Neither guarantees perfect results. Fetch can lose text or structure because of OCR and layout limitations. Media Descriptions can omit details or introduce incorrect interpretations because its output is model-generated. Verify consequential details against the original source and compare the billing paths in the pricing section below.

## Choose an integration

| Integration | When to use it |
| --- | --- |
| Fetch API | Your application controls which URLs or inline base64 data URIs to process and needs structured results, processing-unit usage, and per-item errors. |
| [Web utilities MCP](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/mcp-utilities/web-utilities-mcp.md) | An MCP-compatible client needs to read public URLs through `fetch_url`. This tool accepts one to five URLs per call. |
| [Built-in tools](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/tools/builtin-tools.md) | An AIVAX model needs to read a URL during inference. Enable `OpenUrl` and follow the URL Context configuration guide. |

The integrations have different input contracts. In particular, the MCP tool accepts public URLs; use the Fetch API for inline base64 data URIs. For a backend pipeline that chains search and fetch and keeps an evidence record, see [web search API for LLM agents](https://aivax.net/blog/research-is-a-pipeline-search-discovers-fetch-reads/).

## Fetch content with the API

Authenticate with an AIVAX API key; see [Authentication](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/authentication.md). Supply a non-empty `contents` array containing URLs or base64 data URIs. Each item is subject to a size limit (see [Pricing and limits](#pricing-and-limits)).

The `system.v1.web.fetch` operation accepts these JSON request fields:

| Field | Type | Required | Behavior |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `contents` | Array of strings | Yes | Non-empty list of URLs or base64 data URIs to extract. |
| `returnErrors` | Boolean | No | Defaults to `true`: includes a result for each failed item. When `false`, failed items are omitted. |
| `responseSchema` | JSON Schema object | No | Converts each item's extracted text into JSON guided by this schema. Omit it or use `null` for text-only extraction. The same schema applies to every item in the batch. |
| `responseSchema.instructions` | String | No | Optional extraction guidance inside the schema, such as which details to select or how to handle missing information. This is an AIVAX extension, not a standard JSON Schema keyword. |

### Extract structured JSON

Provide `responseSchema` when your application needs fields from the source rather than only its text. Describe the expected properties, types, and required fields with JSON Schema. Use property descriptions and optional `responseSchema.instructions` to clarify what to extract. For example, an object schema can request a receipt's merchant, date, and total; the embedded reference includes a complete JSON request example.

JSON conversion runs after text extraction. Successful results retain `extractedText` alongside `extractedObject`, so you can compare the generated fields with the extracted source. Without a schema, no JSON conversion runs.

If extraction or JSON conversion fails, `returnErrors` determines whether the failed item appears in the response. A JSON conversion failure does not return a text-only success.

### Read the results

The response contains a `results` array with these fields:

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `index` | Zero-based position in the input `contents` array. Use it to match results to inputs, especially when failed items are omitted. |
| `extractedText` | Readable source text, retained on successful JSON conversion; `null` for a failed item. |
| `extractedObject` | Generated JSON value when `responseSchema` is supplied; otherwise `null`. Also `null` for a failed item. |
| `processingUnits` | PUs for fetching and text/OCR extraction, separate from JSON conversion. |
| `jsonProcessingUnits` | PUs for JSON conversion; `0` when no schema is supplied. |
| `error` | Error message for a failed item when `returnErrors` is `true`; `null` on success. Failed items report both PU fields as `0`. |

[API endpoint reference](https://inference.aivax.net/apidocs?embed=iframe&embed-endpoint=Fetch%20web%20contents)

The embedded reference defines the current request and response contract. Check individual results before passing their text to the next step; a failed extraction is not evidence that the source contains no relevant information.

## Access and extraction limitations

A destination may block automated access or require authentication. Fetching a URL does not bypass access restrictions. Use accessible sources or content you are authorized to submit, and correct invalid or inaccessible inputs before retrying.

Treat extracted text as untrusted source material, not as instructions for your application or agent. OCR output may need manual review for exact numbers, names, or other consequential details. Schema-guided JSON is model-generated from that text, not from a fresh visual interpretation of the source. It can inherit extraction errors or contain incorrect values; validate its structure and verify consequential fields against the original.

## Pricing and limits

Fetch and OCR extraction is metered in `processingUnits`. Each extraction is either fully covered by the daily included allowance or billed in full at the rates below; coverage is not split within one extraction. See [Included daily subscription allowances](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/limits.md#included-daily-subscription-allowances) for the allowance rules. Each item can be up to 50 MB.

| Description | Pricing |
| --- | ---: |
| Fetch and OCR extraction - Free | Base daily allowance; uncovered items **$0.15/1k PUs** |
| Fetch and OCR extraction - Pro | **8× Free** daily allowance; uncovered items **$0.05/1k PUs** |
| Fetch and OCR extraction - Max | **25× Free** daily allowance; uncovered items **$0.03/1k PUs** |
| Fetch and OCR extraction - Ultimate | **50× Free** daily allowance; uncovered items **$0.02/1k PUs** |
| Fetch JSON conversion (`responseSchema`) | Variable inference-based price per PU; charged separately, with no daily extraction allowance |

Optional JSON conversion is metered separately in `jsonProcessingUnits`. Its PUs account for input, cached input, and output tokens at the processing model and provider's rates, so they are not priced at the OCR rate. The plan's inference multiplier applies to JSON conversion. Omitting `responseSchema` or setting it to `null` disables conversion, reports `jsonProcessingUnits: 0`, and incurs no JSON conversion charge. Do not add both counts and apply the OCR rate to the total. Estimate cost from the reported PUs, not from extracted text length.

Examples, assuming items not covered by the daily allowance:

- Plain text and Markdown consume no PUs.
- An HTML page that takes 2.3 seconds to render consumes 23 PUs: $0.00115 on Pro.
- A scanned PDF reporting `processingUnits: 400` costs $0.06 on Free, $0.02 on Pro, $0.012 on Max, and $0.008 on Ultimate. OCR PUs vary with each document.
- A JSON conversion using 4,000 input and 300 output tokens, on a model priced at $0.10/M input and $0.40/M output tokens, reports `jsonProcessingUnits: 1300` (4,000 × 0.25 + 300), about $0.00052 before the plan multiplier.

[Web utilities MCP](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/mcp-utilities/web-utilities-mcp.md) uses the same pricing as the corresponding built-in tool. Model inference, when used to analyze the extracted content, is billed separately. The Fetch API requires a positive account balance.

---

Source: https://docs.aivax.net/docs/generations/images.html

# Image Generation

Use Image Generation to create images from a text prompt in an application workflow. Typical uses include draft illustrations for editorial review, product mockups, marketing variations for A/B testing, and placeholder art that a designer refines later.

Authenticate requests with an AIVAX API key. See [Authentication](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/authentication.md) for authorization guidance.

## Choose a model

Select an image-generation model available to the authenticated account. Model availability and capabilities can change, so obtain current options from the platform instead of depending on a fixed list in this guide.

When several models are available, compare them by capability:

- **Reference images:** only some models accept `referenceImages`.
- **Variations:** decide how many images you need per prompt; `count` accepts 1 to 4.
- **Wait time:** image requests on some models take a while. For those, send the request to `https://direct.inference.aivax.net` and raise your client timeout, as described in [long-running inference](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/overview.md#long-running-inference).

## Generate an image

Use prompts that state the outcome you need rather than relying on vague visual labels. Include the important details, such as the subject, environment, framing, and any text that must be present. One request can carry a single prompt or an array of prompts. Each prompt generates `count` images, and their URLs come back grouped by input prompt.

Control the output with these optional fields:

- `size`: the image dimensions, either as a `"1024x1024"` string or as `{ "width": 1024, "height": 1024 }`. Each side must be between 64 and 4096 pixels. The default is 1080×1920. The model may adjust the size to dimensions it supports, so check the delivered image.
- `format`: `png`, `jpeg` or `webp`. When omitted, the image keeps the format produced by the model.
- `quality`: an integer from 1 to 100 that sets the `jpeg` or `webp` encoding quality. It has no effect on `png`. When the image is converted and `quality` is omitted, 90 is used.

Each prompt group returns `images`, the URLs of the delivered images, and `outputs`, one entry per requested image in request order. Each entry has the image `url`, the `cost` charged for it and, when it failed, an `error` message with a `null` URL. The group `cost` is the sum charged for that prompt. A request can succeed with some failed images, so check `outputs` rather than assuming `images` has `count` entries.

Supply up to four HTTP(S) reference images when the selected model supports them and the output must follow an existing subject, style, or composition. References guide the result; they do not guarantee identity preservation, so inspect the output before publishing.

Treat generated assets as drafts and review them for accuracy, brand suitability, and unintended content before release. When the first result is close but not right, iterate by tightening one element at a time — subject detail, composition, style constraint — rather than rewriting the whole prompt at once.

The embedded reference is the source of truth for the request shape, supported options, and response fields.

[API endpoint reference](https://inference.aivax.net/apidocs?embed=iframe&embed-endpoint=Generate%20images)

To let an MCP-compatible agent or IDE generate images without calling this endpoint directly, use the [Media generation MCP](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/mcp-utilities/media-generation-mcp.md). For a Claude Code setup, see [generate images in Claude Code with an MCP server](https://aivax.net/blog/generate-images-and-speech-from-claude-code-with-mcp/).

## Pricing, limits, and errors

Image generation is charged per delivered image, with an additional charge per reference image on some models. Failed or undelivered outputs are not charged. Each output is priced at the selected model's fixed output tariff, plus that model's per-reference tariff for every reference image sent with it. Prompt processing is included. For token- and megapixel-priced providers, the charge uses rounded-up estimates rather than exact provider-cost pass-through. No additional AIVAX image-generation markup or account and plan multiplier applies. Current tariffs for each model are listed in the Models catalog.

The built-in image generation and editing tool has a daily limit that depends on the plan; see [Built-in tools and web search limits](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/limits.md#built-in-tools-and-web-search).

If a request fails, revise the reported validation issue before retrying.

---

Source: https://docs.aivax.net/docs/generations/speech.html

# Text-to-Speech (TTS)

Use Speech Generation when your application already has final text and needs playable audio without running a chat completion. Typical uses include narrating an article or notification, voicing an IVR prompt, producing a draft voice-over for review, or generating audio files for offline playback.

Authenticate requests with an AIVAX API key. See [Authentication](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/authentication.md) for authorization guidance.

## Choose the delivery form

The endpoint can return audio in two forms, and the right choice depends on the consumer:

- **Binary audio (`raw: true`)** — the response body is the audio file itself, served inline with its MIME type. Use this when a player, browser `<audio>` element, or download flow consumes the response directly.
- **Base64 in the JSON envelope (`raw: false`)** — the response contains the format, MIME type, and base64-encoded audio inside the standard envelope. Use this when the result travels through JSON pipelines, gets stored in a database, or needs to be inspected alongside billing metadata.

Supported formats are `mp3`, `wav`, and `ogg`. When the consumer accepts any of them, prefer `mp3` for smaller payloads and `wav` for maximum compatibility with audio tooling.

## Generate speech

Write text that is ready to be spoken aloud, including punctuation and formatting that communicate pauses or emphasis. Expand abbreviations and numerals the way they should be heard, such as "doctor" instead of "Dr." or "twenty twenty-six" instead of "2026", rather than trusting the voice to guess.

Test the selected voice with representative content before using it in production, especially for names, abbreviations, or specialized terms. Voices differ per speech model, so confirm the voice against the model you will use rather than assuming one model's voices exist in another.

The embedded reference is the source of truth for available models and voices, request options, output formats, and response fields.

[API endpoint reference](https://inference.aivax.net/apidocs?embed=iframe&embed-endpoint=Generate%20speech)

To let an MCP-compatible agent or IDE synthesize speech without calling this endpoint directly, use the [Media generation MCP](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/mcp-utilities/media-generation-mcp.md). It returns a public URL to MP3 audio instead of inline audio.

## Speech or Voice Sessions

Use Speech Generation for one-shot synthesis of known text. Use [Voice Sessions](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/inference/voice-session.md) when the experience is an interactive spoken conversation with interruptions, turn-taking, and tool calls. Chaining transcription, inference, and synthesis manually adds latency that the realtime session avoids.

## Pricing, limits, and errors

Speech generation price varies by model; current tariffs are listed in the Models catalog.

Standalone text-to-speech requests are limited per minute, and per hour on Free; see [Speech limits](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/limits.md#speech). Voice Sessions are not subject to these standalone request quotas; they follow the selected realtime model's access, balance, and inference limits. Review reported validation errors before retrying a failed request.

---

Source: https://docs.aivax.net/docs/generations/audio-transcriptions.html

# Speech-to-Text (STT)

Use Audio Transcriptions to convert recorded speech into text for search, review, captions, or downstream automation. Typical uses include transcribing meetings and interviews, captioning recorded videos, making voice notes searchable, and feeding spoken input into classification or RAG pipelines.

Authenticate requests with an AIVAX API key. See [Authentication](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/authentication.md) for authorization guidance.

## Choose a transcription model

Query the available transcription models for the authenticated account before selecting one. Availability can vary by account configuration, so do not hard-code a catalog in your application.

[API endpoint reference](https://inference.aivax.net/apidocs?embed=iframe&embed-endpoint=Get%20Audio%20Transcription%20Models)

## Transcribe audio

Send the audio as base64 with its format (`wav`, `mp3`, `m4a`, `flac`, `ogg`, `webm`, or `aac`). Decoded audio is subject to the size limit in [Pricing, limits, and errors](#pricing-limits-and-errors). Billing follows the measured media duration, and files with no measurable duration are rejected.

Provide the optional `language` hint when the spoken language is known. It steers recognition toward that language and helps with accented speech and domain vocabulary; omit it when the language genuinely varies within one file and let detection handle it.

Review the returned text before using it in user-visible or irreversible actions: noisy recordings, multiple speakers, specialized vocabulary, and poor microphone quality can affect transcription quality. The endpoint returns the transcript text, not speaker labels, so plan a diarization or review step downstream for files where speaker attribution matters.

The embedded reference is the source of truth for accepted request forms, options, and response fields.

[API endpoint reference](https://inference.aivax.net/apidocs?embed=iframe&embed-endpoint=Transcribe%20audio)

## After the transcript

A transcript is usually the start of a pipeline, not the end. Index it into a [RAG collection](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/rag/collections.md) to make recordings searchable, run it through [Batch](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/inference/batch.md) when there are many files, or feed it to [Text classification](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/data-processing/classification.md) to label conversations at scale. For live conversation instead of recorded audio, use [Voice Sessions](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/inference/voice-session.md).

## Pricing, limits, and errors

Transcription price varies by model; current tariffs are listed in the Models catalog.

Standalone audio-transcription requests are limited per minute, and per hour on Free; see [Speech limits](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/limits.md#speech). Transcription requests have a quota separate from speech generation, with the same values. Decoded audio is limited to 75 MB per request. Correct invalid or inaccessible audio before retrying a failed request.

---

Source: https://docs.aivax.net/docs/data-processing/media-descriptions.html

# Media Descriptions

Use Media Descriptions when an application needs structured information from audio, images, video, or PDF content. Typical uses include preparing media for search, moderation review, accessibility workflows, and downstream automation.

Choose the more specialized API when the task is limited to a single medium, such as [Audio Transcriptions](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/generations/audio-transcriptions.md) for speech-to-text.

## Media Descriptions, Extraction, or Fetch

- **Media Descriptions** interprets images, PDFs, audio, and video and returns generated text guided by your instructions. Use it to explain a chart, describe a photo, or answer a question about a video.
- **[Extraction](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/data-processing/extraction.md)** reads text, images, and PDFs and returns the fields defined by your JSON schema, one object per document. Use it when you need the same fields, such as totals or identifiers, from every document. [Summarization](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/data-processing/summarization.md) is its counterpart for short summaries.
- **[Fetch and OCR](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/web-foundation/fetch-and-ocr.md)** returns the readable text of web pages and documents. Use it when you need the full text, for example to index it.

## Describe media or reason over it directly

There are two ways to extract information from media, and they serve different needs:

- **Describe media, then decide** — use this endpoint when you need a reusable text artifact: a description stored for search, a transcript-like record for audit, or input text for a later workflow stage that runs independently.
- **Multimodal inference in one request** — send the media straight to a chat model that supports the input type when the model should reason over it immediately and no intermediate artifact is needed. See [Inference](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/inference/chat-completions/concepts.md).

Prefer Media Descriptions when the extraction guidance is stable and the result feeds several consumers. Prefer direct multimodal inference when the question about the media changes on every request.

## Describe media

Provide media that AIVAX can access, and use guidance that focuses the extraction on the information your workflow needs. The optional `extractionGuidance` instruction narrows the output — "identify the main subject and visible text" for an image, "summarize the sequence of events" for a video — so write it as the question your workflow needs answered.

Each submitted item is handled independently and results come back in input order, so keep the positions aligned when correlating results with the original media. Under the `auto` preset, remote file URLs are downloaded before processing, within a size limit (see [Pricing, limits, and errors](#pricing-limits-and-errors)). Switch to `high` when the service should receive the remote URL directly.

For remote media, make sure the resource remains accessible for the duration of processing and does not require interactive sign-in. Avoid sending credentials, personal data, or other content that must not appear in a generated description.

The embedded reference is the source of truth for accepted media forms, request options, and response fields.

[API endpoint reference](https://inference.aivax.net/apidocs?embed=iframe&embed-endpoint=Describe%20media)

## Pricing, limits, and errors

| Description | Pricing |
| --- | ---: |
| Media descriptions | **~$1.50/M tokens** |

The price is approximate and depends on the available processing model.

Under the `auto` preset, remote files are downloaded by AIVAX up to 5 MB each. The number of requests per minute depends on the plan; see [Data processing limits](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/limits.md#data-processing).

Correct inaccessible media or invalid content before retrying.

---

Source: https://docs.aivax.net/docs/data-processing/decisions.html

# Semantic Decisions

Semantic decisions evaluate named questions against a shared state and return structured answers rather than a generated explanation. Use them to route support requests, select a category, check a condition, or assign an ordered score.

A request supplies the model, the evidence in `state`, and a `questions` object. Each question has an ID you choose; the response uses the same ID in `answers`. You can ask different question types in one request without making separate API calls.

Use [structured responses](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/inference/structured-responses/concepts.md) instead when you need a larger generated object or a written explanation. For embedding-based similarity between documents and labels, see [Text classification](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/data-processing/classification.md).

## Choose a model

All models below support `choice`, `noul`, and `score`. See [Usage and cost](#usage-and-cost) for model rates and [Model-specific limits](#model-specific-limits) for model limits.

| Model |
| --- |
| `@supersonic-labs/julia-1` |
| `@typesafe/jev-1.13` |
| `@typesafe/jev-1.14` |
| `@respan/span-02` |
| `@respan/span-01` |
| `@respan/span-01-lite` |
| `@jaredpalmer/kev-4b` |
| `@upstage/solar-decide` |
| `@cloudflare/clef` |
| `@cloudflare/clef-flash` |
| `@liquid/d1-ultra` |
| `@liquid/d1` |
| `@liquid/d1.1` |
| `@perplexity/pplx-decider-v1.2` |
| `@perplexity/pplx-decider-flash-v1.2` |
| `@openai/gpt-6-luna-decisions` |
| `@microsoft/microsoft-decision-1` |
| `@nace-ai/drex-v1.5` |
| `@nace-ai/drex-v2.0` |
| `@nace-ai/drex-max` |
| `@cloudflare/clef-omni` |
| `@upstage/solar-decide-flash` |
| `@scaledown/classify-1` |
| `@inception/mercury-decide` |

Each response returns the canonical model name in `model`. You can also send one of the short aliases below. Each alias currently resolves to the canonical model shown, but it can move to a newer version when one is released. Pin the canonical name when you need a stable version.

| Alias | Resolves to |
| --- | --- |
| `@supersonic-labs/julia:latest` | `@supersonic-labs/julia-1` |
| `@typesafe/jev:latest` | `@typesafe/jev-1.14` |
| `@respan/span:latest` | `@respan/span-01` |
| `@respan/span-lite:latest` | `@respan/span-01-lite` |
| `@jaredpalmer/kev:latest` | `@jaredpalmer/kev-4b` |
| `@liquid/d:latest` | `@liquid/d1.1` |
| `@perplexity/pplx-decider:latest` | `@perplexity/pplx-decider-v1.2` |
| `@perplexity/pplx-decider-flash:latest` | `@perplexity/pplx-decider-flash-v1.2` |
| `@nace-ai/drex:latest` | `@nace-ai/drex-v1.5` |

An unspecified context limit does not mean unlimited input. Model-specific limits and interpretation of scores can differ; validate a model on representative examples before switching production traffic.

An authenticated API key and a positive account balance are required, including when selecting a model with a zero base token price. See [Authentication](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/authentication.md), [Pricing](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/pricing.md), and [Plans and limits](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/limits.md).

### Discover models programmatically

`GET /api/v1/information/decisions-models.json` lists the current decision-model catalog without authentication. The response's `data` array contains:

- `name`: the canonical identifier to use in a decision request.
- `aliases`: other accepted identifiers for that model.
- `contextLength`: the advertised context in tokens, or `null` when unspecified.
- `maxImages`: the number of images accepted per request, or `0` for text-only models.
- `releaseDate`: the catalog release date in `yyyy-MM-dd` format.
- `capabilities`: supported question types (`noul`, `choice`, and/or `score`).
- `inputPricePerMillionTokens` and `outputPricePerMillionTokens`: base token prices before account and plan adjustments; see [Usage and cost](#usage-and-cost).

Use this listing to populate model selectors rather than maintaining a separate hardcoded catalog. It describes configured models, not a real-time provider health check. Model-specific option and question limits are not included in this listing.

## Write the questions

| Type | `criteria` format | Use it for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `choice` | Object mapping choice IDs to descriptions | Select one destination or category |
| `noul` | Object with nonempty `false` and `true` descriptions | Evaluate a Boolean condition |
| `score` | Ordered array of level descriptions | Evaluate a graded condition |

Every question requires nonempty `instructions`. Use descriptions that distinguish the options, not just opaque IDs. For example, `"billing": "Charges, payments, and refunds"` provides more evidence than `"billing": "B"`.

For `noul`, both criteria are required. Describe what counts as false as carefully as what counts as true, especially when the state might omit the relevant information. For `score`, keep the level order consistent across requests.

## Evaluate a support request

Send the following JSON body to `POST /api/v1/generations/decisions`. The example uses Julia-1; its state may be text, an object, or an array.

```json
{
  "model": "@supersonic-labs/julia-1",
  "state": {
    "message": "I was charged twice. Please return the extra payment."
  },
  "questions": {
    "department": {
      "type": "choice",
      "instructions": "Which team should handle this request?",
      "criteria": {
        "billing": "Charges, payments, and refunds",
        "technical": "Software errors and service outages",
        "sales": "Plans, pricing, and purchases"
      }
    },
    "refund_requested": {
      "type": "noul",
      "instructions": "Does the customer explicitly ask for money back?",
      "criteria": {
        "false": "The customer does not ask for money to be returned",
        "true": "The customer asks for a refund or return of a payment"
      }
    },
    "urgency": {
      "type": "score",
      "instructions": "How urgent is the request based on the stated deadline?",
      "criteria": [
        "No deadline stated",
        "A deadline is stated, but it is not today",
        "The customer explicitly needs resolution today"
      ]
    }
  }
}
```

Tips for reliable answers:

- Keep only relevant evidence in the state.
- Write instructions that explain the decision, not ones that ask for a chain of reasoning or additional text.
- Avoid overlapping choice descriptions unless that ambiguity is intentional.

For a walkthrough with routing code and model prices, see [Decisions API example: triage a support ticket](https://aivax.net/blog/support-triage-typed-decisions/).

### Send images

`@cloudflare/clef`, `@cloudflare/clef-flash`, `@cloudflare/clef-omni`, and `@openai/gpt-6-luna-decisions` accept images. Put each image directly in a top-level `state` array as an `image_url` part, next to text items written as plain strings:

```json
{
  "model": "@cloudflare/clef-omni",
  "state": [
    "Listing title: Red square sticker",
    { "type": "image_url", "image_url": { "url": "data:image/png;base64,<BASE64_IMAGE>" } }
  ],
  "questions": {
    "matches_title": {
      "type": "noul",
      "instructions": "The photo shows the item in the title.",
      "criteria": { "true": "The item in the title is visible", "false": "The item is not visible" }
    }
  }
}
```

- `url` must be a base64 data URL of type `image/png`, `image/jpeg`, or `image/webp`. Remote `http(s)` URLs are not fetched and are rejected.
- Images nested inside objects in `state` are not read as images. A top-level `images` field, `input_image` parts, and base64 without the `data:image/...;base64,` prefix are not supported.
- Only some models accept images, each up to a per-request maximum. Sending images to any other model, or more than the model accepts, returns `400`. See [Model-specific limits](#model-specific-limits).
- Clef and Clef Flash also bound the image size and the amount of text they read from `state`; see the same limits section. Billing uses the input tokens the model processes, as reported in `usage.input_tokens`.

### Read the response

The success response is a JSON object directly, **without a `data` envelope**. It contains:

- `id`: the decision identifier.
- `model`: the canonical model identifier used for the request.
- `provider`: the provider reported for the result.
- `answers`: an object keyed by your question IDs.
- `usage`: `input_tokens`, `output_tokens`, and the billed `cost`.

For Julia-1, an illustrative `answers` object for the example above is shown below. These numbers explain the format; they are not a recorded response or a quality guarantee.

```json
{
  "department": {
    "type": "choice",
    "choice": "billing",
    "probabilities": {
      "billing": 0.90,
      "technical": 0.06,
      "sales": 0.04
    }
  },
  "refund_requested": {
    "type": "noul",
    "noul": 0.95,
    "probabilities": {
      "false": 0.05,
      "true": 0.95
    }
  },
  "urgency": {
    "type": "score",
    "score": 0.3,
    "legend": {
      "0": "No deadline stated",
      "1": "A deadline is stated, but it is not today",
      "2": "The customer explicitly needs resolution today"
    },
    "probabilities": {
      "0": 0.8,
      "1": 0.1,
      "2": 0.1
    }
  }
}
```

With Julia-1:

- `choice` is the selected caller-defined ID, not the option description.
- `noul` is the probability assigned to the true criterion, not a JSON Boolean. Your application chooses the threshold and how to handle uncertain cases.
- `score` is the expected **zero-based level index**. In the example, `0 × 0.8 + 1 × 0.1 + 2 × 0.1 = 0.3`. It is not necessarily an integer, and it is not a normalized 0–1 score when there are more than two levels.
- `probabilities` are keyed by choice IDs, `false`/`true`, or score-level indices. `legend` describes the score levels.

Other models may omit optional fields such as `probabilities`, `legend`, or `confidence`. Do not assume that every provider uses the same score scale or confidence definition. A high probability is not proof that the decision is correct; validate thresholds and escalation rules with labeled examples from your own domain.

## Account rate limits

Semantic decision requests share one per-minute rate limit per account, across all decision models and API keys. Each request consumes one unit, regardless of how many questions it contains or which decision model it selects. The number of requests per minute depends on the plan; see [Data processing limits](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/limits.md#data-processing).

This quota is independent of the daily subscription allowance and of billing: included usage still consumes request units. Ultimate has no plan-imposed limit for this quota, but other applicable limits remain in effect.

Requests above the limit return `429 Too Many Requests` before evaluation. An immediate retry still encounters the active rate-limit window, and changing API keys within the same account does not provide a separate quota. Pace calls across the account and retry with backoff after the window clears.

## Model-specific limits

These model-specific limits apply in addition to the account-level request quota above. An unspecified context limit does not imply unlimited input.

| Model | Context |
| --- | --- |
| `@supersonic-labs/julia-1` | 1,024 tokens per question |
| `@typesafe/jev-1.13` | 262,144 tokens |
| `@typesafe/jev-1.14` | 262,144 tokens |
| `@respan/span-02` | 131,072 tokens |
| `@respan/span-01` | Not specified in the current catalog |
| `@respan/span-01-lite` | Not specified in the current catalog |
| `@jaredpalmer/kev-4b` | 8,192 tokens |
| `@upstage/solar-decide` | 524,288 tokens |
| `@cloudflare/clef` | 65,536 tokens |
| `@cloudflare/clef-flash` | 24,576 tokens |
| `@liquid/d1-ultra` | 32,768 tokens |
| `@liquid/d1` | 65,536 tokens |
| `@liquid/d1.1` | 65,536 tokens |
| `@perplexity/pplx-decider-v1.2` | 262,144 tokens |
| `@perplexity/pplx-decider-flash-v1.2` | 262,144 tokens |
| `@openai/gpt-6-luna-decisions` | 1,050,000 tokens |
| `@microsoft/microsoft-decision-1` | 32,768 tokens |
| `@nace-ai/drex-v1.5` | 131,072 tokens |
| `@cloudflare/clef-omni` | 65,536 tokens |
| `@nace-ai/drex-v2.0` | 131,072 tokens |
| `@nace-ai/drex-max` | 262,144 tokens |
| `@upstage/solar-decide-flash` | 524,288 tokens |
| `@scaledown/classify-1` | 1,000,000 tokens |
| `@inception/mercury-decide` | 65,536 tokens |

Image input per request: `@cloudflare/clef`, `@cloudflare/clef-flash`, and `@cloudflare/clef-omni` accept up to 4 images; `@inception/mercury-decide` accepts up to 16; `@openai/gpt-6-luna-decisions` accepts up to 128. Other decision models are text-only. The `maxImages` field of the model listing is the authoritative value.

`@cloudflare/clef` and `@cloudflare/clef-flash` reject requests that exceed their processing window, so keep each image under about 300 KB before encoding. They also read roughly the first 2,000 tokens of text in `state`; images are counted separately.

Julia-1 has additional serving limits:

| Limit | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Questions per request | 1–32 |
| Choices or score levels per question | 2–20 |
| Boolean options | Exactly two: false and true |
| Combined context per question | 1,024 tokens, including state, question, options, and special tokens |
| Question and options budget | 256 tokens within the combined context |
| Description of an individual option | At most 48 tokens |
| Decision payload limit | 256 KiB |

These limits interact: twenty options can exceed the combined question/options budget even if each description fits its individual limit. The current AIVAX Julia-1 serving limits apply even if an upstream model card lists a larger context. Shorten descriptions or reduce the option count instead of assuming every maximum can be used at once.

Inputs exceeding the context or question/options budget are rejected, not silently truncated. The literal `<mask>` is reserved and cannot appear in Julia-1 state, instructions, or option descriptions.

## Usage and cost

The decision-model rates below are base USD prices per million input tokens, before account and plan adjustments (see the [plan multiplier](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/pricing.md#plan-multipliers)). Output tokens have no charge in the current decision-model catalog. Julia-1 is eligible for the daily allowance described after the table.

| Model | Input price / million tokens |
| --- | ---: |
| `@supersonic-labs/julia-1` | **$0.008** |
| `@typesafe/jev-1.13` | **$0.042** |
| `@typesafe/jev-1.14` | **$0.042** |
| `@respan/span-02` | **$0.010** |
| `@respan/span-01` | **$0.020** |
| `@respan/span-01-lite` | **$0.000** |
| `@jaredpalmer/kev-4b` | **$0.042** |
| `@upstage/solar-decide` | **$0.100** |
| `@cloudflare/clef` | **$0.240** |
| `@cloudflare/clef-flash` | **$0.038** |
| `@liquid/d1-ultra` | **$0.042** |
| `@liquid/d1` | **$0.020** |
| `@liquid/d1.1` | **$0.020** |
| `@perplexity/pplx-decider-v1.2` | **$0.020** |
| `@perplexity/pplx-decider-flash-v1.2` | **$0.010** |
| `@openai/gpt-6-luna-decisions` | **$0.100** |
| `@microsoft/microsoft-decision-1` | **$0.042** |
| `@nace-ai/drex-v1.5` | **$0.040** |
| `@cloudflare/clef-omni` | **$0.150** |
| `@nace-ai/drex-v2.0` | **$0.060** |
| `@nace-ai/drex-max` | **$0.060** |
| `@upstage/solar-decide-flash` | **$0.100** |
| `@scaledown/classify-1` | **$0.050** |
| `@inception/mercury-decide` | **$0.040** |

For Julia-1, input usage sums the encoded sequence for each question, excluding padding. The shared state is therefore counted again for each question, so input usage grows with the number of questions even when they share one state. Julia-1 does not generate text, so its `output_tokens` value is zero.

Julia-1 is currently eligible for the daily semantic decision allowance on every plan. Other decision models are billed normally. The allowance is shared across all eligible decision calls of the account, not reserved for each question or API key. See [Plans and Limits](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/limits.md#included-daily-subscription-allowances) for relative plan capacity and coverage rules.

When not covered, Julia-1 input is billed at the [listed rate](#usage-and-cost), subject to account and plan adjustments. Use the returned `usage.cost` for the actual billed amount; it is zero when the input is fully covered by the allowance.

## Errors and reliable use

- **Invalid model or question:** check the exact model identifier, question type, instructions, and criteria shape. Question IDs and choice IDs must be nonempty.
- **Context or option limit exceeded:** shorten the state or descriptions, reduce the option count, or select a model with suitable limits. Retrying the same invalid input will not resolve it.
- **Authentication or balance error:** verify the API key and account balance before retrying. A zero-priced model still requires a positive balance.
- **Rate limit (429):** reduce the account's request rate and retry with backoff. Multiple questions in one request still count as one request, but model-specific payload limits and per-question usage remain applicable.
- **Temporary capacity or provider unavailability:** avoid an immediate parallel retry storm. Reduce concurrency and use bounded retries with backoff for transient failures.

Evaluate `choice`, `noul`, and `score` separately when validating a model: success at routing does not establish reliable scoring or Boolean behavior. Include ambiguous and incomplete states in your test set, and use human review where a wrong decision has material consequences. A retry is a new request; do not assume automatic deduplication or identical model outputs.

## API reference

[API endpoint reference](https://inference.aivax.net/apidocs?embed=iframe&embed-endpoint=Evaluate%20semantic%20decisions)

Source: https://docs.aivax.net/docs/data-processing/classification.html

# Text Classification

Use text classification to rank a fixed set of labels for one or more documents without training a custom classifier. It fits tasks such as tagging, triage, or routing requests, where the categories are known in advance and you need a similarity ranking rather than a generated answer.

AIVAX embeds every document and label with the default embedding model and compares their vectors using cosine similarity. For each document, it returns every label ordered from the most similar to the least similar.

Before calling this endpoint, [create an API key](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/authentication.md) and make sure the account has a positive balance.

## Endpoint

<div class="request-item post">
    <span>POST</span>
    <span>/api/v1/generations/classify</span>
</div>

## Request behavior

| Property | Type | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `documents` | `string[]` | Yes | One or more non-empty documents to classify. Results preserve this order and each document's zero-based index. |
| `labels` | `string[]` | Yes | One or more non-empty labels. Every label is scored for every document. |

Duplicate documents and labels are preserved. The endpoint always uses the current default embedding model and does not accept a model parameter, score threshold, or result limit.

The following request classifies three documents, one of them in German, against three labels:

```json
{
  "documents": [
    "Compare the total cost of two loans for a principal of $10,000 over 5 years at different annual rates",
    "Erklären Sie die Unterschiede zwischen Merge-Sort und Quicksort-Algorithmen in Bezug auf Zeitkomplexität, Platzkomplexität und Leistung in der Praxis.",
    "Write a poem about the beauty of nature and its healing power on the human soul"
  ],
  "labels": [
    "Creative writing",
    "Complex problem",
    "Simple task"
  ]
}
```

## Read the response

`results` contains one item for each input document. Each `scores` array contains every supplied label, ordered by descending cosine similarity. Labels with equal scores preserve their original order. The example below is abbreviated to the first document:

```json
{
  "results": [
    {
      "index": 0,
      "document": "Compare the total cost of two loans for a principal of $10,000 over 5 years at different annual rates",
      "scores": [
        {
          "label": "Complex problem",
          "score": 0.98828
        },
        {
          "label": "Simple task",
          "score": 0.45272
        },
        {
          "label": "Creative writing",
          "score": 0.06823
        }
      ]
    }
  ]
}
```

A score measures vector similarity, not a calibrated probability. Compare scores within the same request and embedding model rather than interpreting a value as a percentage confidence. Negative scores are valid and remain in the response because the endpoint does not filter labels.

Embedding usage is billed for text that requires inference and is associated with the authenticated API key. Repeated text may be served from an internal cache, reducing latency and costs. Because the endpoint returns every document-label pair, response size and comparison work grow with `documents × labels`.

## Pricing and limits

Text classification uses the default embedding model and is billed for the embedding work performed.

| Description | Pricing |
| --- | ---: |
| Text classification | **$0.015/M tokens** |

The number of classified documents per minute and per day depends on the plan; see [Data processing limits](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/limits.md#data-processing). The quota counts every item in the request's `documents` array, not each HTTP request. A request that would exceed any active window returns `429 Too Many Requests`.

The embedded API reference contains the server-maintained request, response, authentication, and error details:

[API endpoint reference](https://inference.aivax.net/apidocs?embed=iframe&embed-endpoint=Classify%20documents)

---

Source: https://docs.aivax.net/docs/data-processing/text-segmentation.html

# Text Segmentation

Text segmentation divides source documents into semantically cohesive strings that can be embedded or indexed in a RAG collection. It returns segments to your application; it does not create embeddings or store submitted documents.

Use it when a source document needs reviewable, retrieval-ready boundaries before you create or update collection documents. If you already have focused, self-contained text, you can import it directly. If you want AIVAX to process source files into collection documents, see [Media Injector](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/rag/documents.md#import-from-files-with-media-injector). For a full walkthrough that turns a PDF into segmented, importable chunks, see [PDF to Markdown for RAG](https://aivax.net/blog/pdf-to-markdown-for-rag-chunks-jsonl/).

To see how segmentation relates to storage, updates, and retrieval, read [where segmentation fits in a RAG pipeline](https://aivax.net/blog/a-vector-database-is-not-a-rag-system/).

## Skip segmentation when the text is already focused

Segmentation earns its keep on long, multi-topic sources — manuals, articles, transcripts — where one embedding per page would blur distinct subjects together. Do not segment text that is already one idea per unit: FAQ answers, product descriptions, short policies, or pre-chunked passages can go straight into the collection. Each unnecessary split adds indexing work and risks separating statements that only make sense together.

## What makes a good segment

A good segment is the smallest span that still answers a question on its own: a complete statement or a tight group of statements about one subtopic, typically a paragraph or a short section. Segments are most useful when the source has clear headings, paragraphs, and complete statements — the segmenter preserves those boundaries instead of cutting mid-thought.

Watch the failure modes of messy sources. Tables lose their headers, OCR drops line structure, transcripts ramble across topics, and exported documents repeat running headers on every page. Review results from those sources before indexing, and prefer cleaning the source (fixing headings, removing boilerplate) over asking the segmenter to guess around it.

## Prepare source text

Supply complete source text whenever possible, cleaned as described above.

Without sanitization, segments target about 300 tokens and cover the whole document in source order, without overlap. Boundaries follow the document structure and the semantic similarity of neighboring passages; documents of about that size or smaller are returned as one segment.

Use sanitization only when omitted content is genuinely irrelevant to retrieval. Sanitized requests are processed by a language model and take longer. When exact source wording, legal fidelity, or full traceability matters, retain and review the source text instead.

For the supported request, response, authentication, and error contract, use the API Reference:

[API endpoint reference](https://inference.aivax.net/apidocs?embed=iframe&embed-endpoint=Segment%20text)

## Pricing and limits

| Description | Pricing |
| --- | ---: |
| Text segmentation | **$0.10/M tokens** |

The number of segmented documents per minute and per day depends on the plan; see [Data processing limits](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/limits.md#data-processing). The quota counts every item in the request's `documents` array, not each HTTP request. A request that would exceed any active window returns `429 Too Many Requests`.

---

Source: https://docs.aivax.net/docs/data-processing/extraction.html

# Extraction

Use Extraction to turn text, images, and PDFs into JSON shaped by a schema you define. It fits invoices, receipts, forms, contracts, and other documents where your application needs the same fields from every document, such as a number, a company name, a total, or a list of line items.

Before calling this endpoint, [create an API key](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/authentication.md) and make sure the account has a positive balance.

## Extraction, Fetch, or Media Descriptions

These three services read documents, but they return different things:

| | Extraction | [Fetch and OCR](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/web-foundation/fetch-and-ocr.md) | [Media Descriptions](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/data-processing/media-descriptions.md) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Main purpose | Find specific fields in each document and return them as JSON. | Retrieve the readable text of web pages and documents, using OCR when needed. | Interpret media with AI and return a text description guided by your instructions. |
| Input | Text, JPEG, PNG, TIFF, and PDF content. | Web pages and many document formats, including Office files, spreadsheets, and e-books. | Images, PDFs, audio, and video. |
| Output | One JSON object per document, shaped by your schema. | Extracted text, plus optional JSON converted from that text. | Generated text. |
| Billing | Input tokens only. | Processing units with daily plan allowances; JSON conversion is billed separately. | AI usage charges for input and output. |

Choose Extraction when you already know which fields you need and want them read directly from the document. Choose Fetch when you need the document's full text, for example to index it or to read a web page. Choose Media Descriptions when you need an explanation of visual or audiovisual content, such as a chart, a photo, or a video, rather than specific fields.

## Endpoint

<div class="request-item post">
    <span>POST</span>
    <span>/api/v1/generations/extract</span>
</div>

## Build the request

| Property | Type | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `responseSchema` | JSON Schema object | Yes | Object schema whose `properties` describe the fields to extract. It must have at least one property. |
| `documents` | Content part array | Yes | One or more documents as OpenAI-compatible content parts: `text`, `image_url`, or `file`. |
| `instructions` | String | No | Guidance that applies to every document, such as which party counts as the vendor. |

Each property in `responseSchema` is one field to find. Its `description` is the search criterion, so write it as a short, specific definition, such as "total amount due" instead of "total". Nested objects and arrays of objects are supported. `$ref` and `$defs` are not; inline every definition instead.


Images and files accept base64 data URLs or public HTTP(S) URLs:

- Supported formats are JPEG, PNG, TIFF, and PDF, including multi-page PDFs.
- AIVAX downloads remote URLs before processing, within the file size limit in [Pricing and limits](#pricing-and-limits). The resource must be reachable without sign-in.
- Other content types, such as audio or video, return `400 Bad Request`. The error does not identify which document was rejected, so check the content type of each document in the request.





The following request extracts invoice fields from a text document and a PDF:

```json
{
  "instructions": "Only consider the issuing company as the vendor.",
  "responseSchema": {
    "type": "object",
    "properties": {
      "invoice_number": { "type": "string", "description": "invoice number" },
      "vendor": { "type": "string", "description": "company that issued the invoice" },
      "total": { "type": "number", "description": "total amount due" },
      "line_items": {
        "type": "array",
        "items": {
          "type": "object",
          "properties": {
            "product": { "type": "string", "description": "product name" },
            "quantity": { "type": "integer", "description": "number of units" }
          }
        }
      }
    }
  },
  "documents": [
    {
      "type": "text",
      "text": "Invoice 1042 from Acme Corp. 2 x Widget at $10.00. Total: 20.00 USD."
    },
    {
      "type": "file",
      "file": {
        "filename": "invoice.pdf",
        "file_data": "https://example.com/invoice.pdf"
      }
    }
  ]
}
```

## Read the response

`data` contains one object per document, in the same order as `documents`. Each object uses the property names from your schema. Values are converted to the `number`, `integer`, or `boolean` type declared in the schema when possible. A field that is not found is `null`, and an array with no matches is empty.

```json
{
  "message": null,
  "data": [
    {
      "invoice_number": "1042",
      "vendor": "Acme Corp",
      "total": 20,
      "line_items": [
        { "product": "Widget", "quantity": 2 }
      ]
    }
  ]
}
```

Documents are processed independently and in parallel. If any document fails, the whole request returns an error instead of partial results. Correct or remove that document and retry. Documents that finished before the failure are still billed and count toward your quota, so retry only after fixing the failing document.

Extracted values are model-generated. They can be missing, incomplete, or wrong, especially in low-quality scans or complex layouts. Validate the structure and verify consequential values, such as amounts and identifiers, against the original document.

## Pricing and limits

Extraction is billed for the input tokens of each document. Output tokens are not billed.

| Description | Pricing |
| --- | ---: |
| Extraction input | **$0.04/M tokens** |

Extraction and [Summarization](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/data-processing/summarization.md) share the same document limits. Remote files are downloaded up to 5 MB each. The number of processed documents per minute and per day depends on the plan; see [Data processing limits](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/limits.md#data-processing).

The quota counts every item in the request's `documents` array, not each HTTP request. A request that would exceed any active window returns `429 Too Many Requests`.

The embedded API reference contains the server-maintained request, response, authentication, and error details:

[API endpoint reference](https://inference.aivax.net/apidocs?embed=iframe&embed-endpoint=Extract%20data%20from%20documents)

---

Source: https://docs.aivax.net/docs/data-processing/summarization.html

# Summarization

Use Summarization to condense text, images, and PDFs into short summaries, optionally guided by instructions about format, focus, language, or length. It fits reports, articles, contracts, and scanned documents that need a quick overview before review, search, or a later workflow step.

A summary restates the document in new words without adding information or commentary. To get specific fields as JSON, use [Extraction](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/data-processing/extraction.md) instead. To ask open questions about media or describe visual content, use [Media Descriptions](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/data-processing/media-descriptions.md).

Before calling this endpoint, [create an API key](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/authentication.md) and make sure the account has a positive balance.

## Endpoint

<div class="request-item post">
    <span>POST</span>
    <span>/api/v1/generations/summarize</span>
</div>

## Request behavior

| Property | Type | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `documents` | Content part array | Yes | One or more documents as OpenAI-compatible content parts: `text`, `image_url`, or `file`. |
| `instructions` | String | No | Guidance that applies to every summary, such as format, language, focus, or length. |

Images and files accept base64 data URLs or public HTTP(S) URLs. Supported formats are JPEG, PNG, TIFF, and PDF, including multi-page PDFs. AIVAX downloads remote URLs before processing, within the file size limit in [Pricing and limits](#pricing-and-limits); the resource must be reachable without sign-in. Other content types, such as audio or video, return `400 Bad Request`. The error does not identify which document was rejected, so check the content type of each document in the request.

```json
{
  "instructions": "Answer in three bullet points, in English.",
  "documents": [
    {
      "type": "file",
      "file": {
        "filename": "bitcoin.pdf",
        "file_data": "https://bitcoin.org/bitcoin.pdf"
      }
    }
  ]
}
```

## Read the response

`data` contains one summary string per document, in the same order as `documents`. Documents are summarized independently and in parallel; to get a single summary of several documents, send them as one text document or summarize the individual summaries in a second request.

```json
{
  "message": null,
  "data": [
    "- Proposes a peer-to-peer electronic cash system that works without a trusted third party.\n- Prevents double spending with a proof-of-work chain of timestamped transactions.\n- Stays secure while honest nodes control most of the computing power."
  ]
}
```

If any document fails, the request returns an error instead of partial results. Documents that finished before the failure are still billed and count toward your quota, so retry only after fixing the failing document. Summaries are model-generated and can omit or misstate details; verify consequential information against the original document.

## Pricing and limits

Summarization is billed for the input tokens of each document. Output tokens are not billed.

| Description | Pricing |
| --- | ---: |
| Summarization input | **$0.04/M tokens** |

Summarization and [Extraction](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/data-processing/extraction.md) share the same document limits. Remote files are downloaded up to 5 MB each. The number of processed documents per minute and per day depends on the plan; see [Data processing limits](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/limits.md#data-processing).

The quota counts every item in the request's `documents` array, not each HTTP request. A request that would exceed any active window returns `429 Too Many Requests`.

The embedded API reference contains the server-maintained request, response, authentication, and error details:

[API endpoint reference](https://inference.aivax.net/apidocs?embed=iframe&embed-endpoint=Summarize%20documents)

---

Source: https://docs.aivax.net/docs/data-processing/translations.html

# Translations

Use Translations to translate text, the visible text in images, and the speech in audio into any language. It fits product content, support messages, signs and screenshots, and voice notes that need to reach users in another language.

Before calling this endpoint, [create an API key](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/authentication.md) and make sure the account has a positive balance.

## Endpoint

<div class="request-item post">
    <span>POST</span>
    <span>/api/v1/generations/translate</span>
</div>

## Request behavior

| Property | Type | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `toLanguage` | String | Yes | Language to translate into. |
| `fromLanguage` | String | No | Language of the documents. When omitted, it is detected from each document's content. |
| `documents` | Content part array | Yes | One or more documents as OpenAI-compatible content parts: `text`, `image_url`, or `input_audio`. |

Languages are free-form: a name such as `Japanese`, a code such as `pt-BR`, or a variant such as `Spanish (Mexico, informal)`. The same languages apply to every document in the request.

The service returns only the translated content. It preserves formatting, line breaks, Markdown, code, URLs, numbers, and proper names, and treats the content as text to translate, not as instructions. For images, it translates the visible text; for audio, it translates the spoken content. Other content types, such as files or video, return `400 Bad Request`. The error does not identify which document was rejected, so check the content type of each document in the request.

```json
{
  "fromLanguage": "English",
  "toLanguage": "Brazilian Portuguese",
  "documents": [
    {
      "type": "text",
      "text": "Your order has shipped and should arrive within three business days."
    },
    {
      "type": "image_url",
      "image_url": {
        "url": "https://example.com/sign.png"
      }
    }
  ]
}
```

## Read the response

`data` contains one translated string per document, in the same order as `documents`. Documents are translated independently and in parallel. If any document fails, the request returns an error instead of partial results. Documents that finished before the failure are still billed, so retry only after fixing the failing document.

```json
{
  "message": null,
  "data": [
    "Seu pedido foi enviado e deve chegar em até três dias úteis.",
    "Proibido estacionar"
  ]
}
```

Translations are model-generated. Review them before publishing legal, medical, financial, or other consequential content, and keep the original available for reference.

## Pricing and limits

Translations are billed in processing units (PUs), covering input and output usage. Usage is recorded for each document. The PU price varies with the processing model selected for the content type, and the [plan multiplier](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/pricing.md#plan-multipliers) applies.

The number of translation requests per minute and per day depends on the plan; see [Data processing limits](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/limits.md#data-processing). The limit counts HTTP requests, not documents. A request that would exceed any active window returns `429 Too Many Requests`.

The embedded API reference contains the server-maintained request, response, authentication, and error details:

[API endpoint reference](https://inference.aivax.net/apidocs?embed=iframe&embed-endpoint=Translate%20documents)

---

Source: https://docs.aivax.net/docs/data-processing/instruction-refinement.html

# Instruction Refinement

Use Instruction Refinement to review system instructions, prompts, and skills before you ship them to a model. The service checks them against a catalog of prompt engineering guidelines compiled from model vendors' documentation, then returns a score, prioritized problems located in your text, the guidelines behind each problem, and suggested fixes with patches you can preview and apply.

It fits prompt reviews in pull requests, audits of AI gateway instructions and skills, and editors that highlight problems as you write. It reports guideline issues; it does not run your prompt or measure how a model performs with it. To test behavior against real conversations, use [Agentic Tests](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/inference/agentic-tests.md).

Before calling this endpoint, [create an API key](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/authentication.md) and make sure the account has a positive balance.

## Endpoint

<div class="request-item post">
    <span>POST</span>
    <span>/api/v1/generations/instruction-refinement</span>
</div>

## Choose a view

The review runs in one of two views. Each request runs one view and is billed separately, so run both when you want a complete review.

- **`micro`** (default) reviews the wording inside each item: clarity, measurable constraints, structure, examples, emphasis, tool guidance, output format, and similar guidelines. Use it while writing or editing a single prompt.
- **`macro`** reviews how the items work together as one agent. It checks that the agent has a clear purpose and limits of authority, that each behavior lives in a single item responsible for it, that skills can be selected from their descriptions without overlapping or being forced, that the context matches the tools the agent really has, and that it avoids over-specification such as scripted conversations or rules the platform already provides. Use it when you review a whole agent or its skill set.

The macro view needs the related items to judge relationships. Send the base instructions together with the skills, tool descriptions, and knowledge the agent uses; a single item gives it little to compare.

## Request behavior

| Property | Type | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `view` | String | No | `micro` or `macro`. Defaults to `micro`. |
| `purpose` | String | No | What the agent is meant to achieve. When omitted, the review infers it from the instructions and documentation, and the summary says so. |
| `context` | Object array | Yes | One or more context items, reviewed together. |
| `context[].type` | String | Yes | The item type, described below. |
| `context[].title` | String | No | A label for the item, such as a file or skill name. |
| `context[].description` | String | No | A description of the item. For skills, send the description the agent uses to select the skill, so the review can check whether it activates when needed. |
| `context[].content` | String | Yes | The item text. Must not be empty. |

| Type | Use for |
| --- | --- |
| `instruction` | System or developer instructions that are always loaded. |
| `prompt` | A prompt sent in the user turn. |
| `skill` | An instruction bundle the agent loads on demand. |
| `tool` | The definition or description of a tool available to the agent. |
| `knowledge` | Factual reference content available to the agent, such as products, contacts, or policies. |
| `documentation` | Notes for people about the agent. The agent never sees them. |

Send in one request the items that the same agent receives. A guideline can be satisfied by another item, and findings can point out items that conflict with or duplicate each other; reviewing items in separate requests misses those relationships. In the micro view, `knowledge` and `documentation` items are used only as context.

An unknown `view` or `type`, an empty `content`, or an empty `context` array returns `400 Bad Request`.

```json
{
  "view": "macro",
  "purpose": "Answer billing questions and hand refunds to the finance team.",
  "context": [
    {
      "type": "instruction",
      "title": "support-agent.md",
      "content": "You are a support agent.\nNever promise refunds."
    },
    {
      "type": "skill",
      "title": "refunds",
      "description": "Refunds.",
      "content": "Promise a refund when the customer asks for one."
    }
  ]
}
```

## Read the response

`data` contains the review of all items:

| Property | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `overallScore` | Number | Overall quality from `0` to `1`. Scores below `0.4` mean at least one `P0` finding; scores near `1` mean only minor improvements apply. |
| `summary` | String | A short assessment of the context and its most important improvement. |
| `findings` | Object array | The problems found, up to 20. Can be empty when the context has no relevant problems. |
| `suggestedFixes` | Object array | Concrete changes that resolve one or more findings. In the macro view, conflicts and risks come first. |

Each finding has these properties:

| Property | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `id` | Integer | Identifier of the finding, referenced by `suggestedFixes[].refFinding`. |
| `priority` | String | `P0` for problems that can cause an improper or irreversible action, a regulatory or privacy risk, or leave the agent without identity or purpose; `P1` for likely recurring wrong decisions; `P2` for localized quality loss; `P3` for clarity or organization improvements. |
| `title` | String | Short name of the problem. |
| `description` | String | The problem and its effect on the agent. |
| `locations` | Object array | Every item the finding involves, such as both sides of a conflict. Each location has the `contextIndex` of the item in `context` (zero-based) and an `evidenceSpan`. Can be empty when the problem is not tied to an item. |
| `sources` | Object array | Guidelines that support the finding, described below. |

`evidenceSpan` gives the location of the problem in that item's `content` as `fromLine`, `toLine`, `fromColumn`, and `toColumn`, all 1-based and inclusive. It is `null` when the problem is an omission, when it lies in a skill's `description`, or when the cited text could not be located. Columns count characters from the start of the line, so line breaks inside `content` must match the text you display when you highlight a span.

Each source has an `id` that identifies the guideline in its catalog, a `number` within its type, a `type`, and `references` with the vendor documentation URLs behind it. `type` reflects the guideline's weight: a `rule` prevents predictable failures, a `practice` reliably improves results, a `tip` is optional and situational, and a `dont` is an anti-pattern to avoid. Some macro guidelines cover agent design rather than vendor guidance and have an empty `references` array.

Each suggested fix has a `refFinding` array with the finding ids it resolves, a `description` of exactly what to change and in which item, a `patches` array described below, and a `type`:

| Type | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `modify` | Rewrite the text in place. |
| `remove` | Delete redundant, conflicting, or harmful text. |
| `transfer` | Move the text to another item or type, such as from the instructions into a skill. The description names the destination. |
| `add` | Write content that is missing. The description names the item that should hold it. |

`patches` holds the fix as text changes. Each patch has the `contextIndex` of the item it changes and a `diff` in unified diff format, with three lines of context, against the `content` you sent for that item. The file names in the `---` and `+++` headers are the item's `title` prefixed with `a/` and `b/`, or `context-<index>` when the item has no title. Header lines end with a line feed, and content lines keep the line endings of your `content`. A fix that changes several items, such as a `transfer`, has one patch per item; apply them together.

`patches` is empty when the fix can't be written as a change to the items you sent: it needs content that isn't there, such as a new skill or a tool, it needs facts only you have, such as a limit or a contact, or the text to change couldn't be located unambiguously. Use the `description` in those cases.

Every patch is computed against the original `content`, independently of the other fixes, so two fixes can change the same lines. Apply patches one fix at a time; when a patch no longer applies because an earlier one changed the same text, skip it or request a new review.

`title`, `description`, `summary`, and fix descriptions are written in the language used by most of the analyzed content.

```json
{
  "message": null,
  "data": {
    "overallScore": 0.35,
    "summary": "The instructions and the refunds skill contradict each other about refunds, and the skill description is too vague to be selected reliably.",
    "findings": [
      {
        "id": 1,
        "priority": "P0",
        "title": "Contradictory refund authority",
        "description": "The instructions forbid promising refunds while the skill requires it, so the agent may promise refunds it cannot grant.",
        "locations": [
          {
            "contextIndex": 0,
            "evidenceSpan": { "fromLine": 2, "toLine": 2, "fromColumn": 1, "toColumn": 22 }
          },
          {
            "contextIndex": 1,
            "evidenceSpan": { "fromLine": 1, "toLine": 1, "fromColumn": 1, "toColumn": 48 }
          }
        ],
        "sources": [
          {
            "id": "B.D. 3",
            "number": 3,
            "type": "dont",
            "references": [
              "https://cookbook.openai.com/examples/gpt-5/gpt-5_prompting_guide"
            ]
          }
        ]
      }
    ],
    "suggestedFixes": [
      {
        "refFinding": [ 1 ],
        "type": "modify",
        "description": "In the refunds skill, replace the promise with: \"Explain that the finance team reviews refunds and transfer the request to them.\"",
        "patches": [
          {
            "contextIndex": 1,
            "diff": "--- a/refunds\n+++ b/refunds\n@@ -1,1 +1,1 @@\n-Promise a refund when the customer asks for one.\n\\ No newline at end of file\n+Explain that the finance team reviews refunds and transfer the request to them.\n\\ No newline at end of file\n"
          }
        ]
      }
    ]
  }
}
```

Reviews are model-generated. The score and findings can vary between requests for the same content, and a finding can be wrong or miss context that only you have. A suggested removal can still drop a business rule the review didn't recognize as critical, so check removals against your requirements, read each patch before applying it, and confirm that the changed agent still behaves as expected.

## Pricing and limits

Instruction Refinement is billed in processing units (PUs), covering input and output usage. Usage is recorded once per request. The PU price varies with the processing model that serves the request, and the [plan multiplier](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/pricing.md#plan-multipliers) applies. Longer context items consume more input.

Instruction Refinement shares the document limits of [Extraction](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/data-processing/extraction.md) and [Summarization](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/data-processing/summarization.md). Each item in the request's `context` array counts as one document, not each HTTP request. The number of processed documents per minute and per day depends on the plan; see [Data processing limits](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/limits.md#data-processing). A request that would exceed any active window returns `429 Too Many Requests`.

The embedded API reference contains the server-maintained request, response, authentication, and error details:

[API endpoint reference](https://inference.aivax.net/apidocs?embed=iframe&embed-endpoint=Refine%20instructions)

---

Source: https://docs.aivax.net/docs/tools/builtin-tools.html

# Built-in Tools

Built-in tools are capabilities maintained by AIVAX, such as web search, URL reading, code execution, memory, and file generation, that you can enable for a model without writing your own callback. You can combine them with your own [protocol functions](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/tools/protocol-functions.md) and [MCP](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/tools/mcp.md) tools.

Some tools have usage charges. See [Pricing and limits](#pricing-and-limits) before enabling them in a production workflow.
